title: Car rental management
alt: Actual Fleetdesk dashboard with eight synthetic vehicles, six fictional customers and calculated example rates
desc: A polished workspace for vehicle inventory and customer records, with a tested Flask API and an explicitly static public demonstration.
built: Developed the original Flask/MySQL coursework into a practical record-management dashboard with a shared browser demonstration.
why: Everyday record management depends on clear workflows and consistent data. This prototype brings the interface, API and storage responsibilities together.
how: Browse synthetic vehicles and customers, with summaries calculated from current records.
Create, search, edit and delete records with clear validation, cancellation and confirmation.
Reset the sample workspace, or run the same frontend against the local Flask API and optional MySQL store.
demonstrates: Full-stack development, REST endpoints, relational data access and translating a record-management requirement into a usable interface.
caption: The verified Fleetdesk dashboard: eight synthetic vehicles, six fictional customers and a calculated €59 mean daily rate. This image is captured from the source revision shown below.
result: 13 API/authentication regression tests, an isolated MySQL 8.4 CRUD/authentication integration test, two frontend-rule tests and three browser workflow tests passed before this release. Browser checks cover both Flask and static modes, persistence, duplicates, cancellation, reset, simulated failure recovery and mobile layout. The linked run records the exact revision.
limits: All public records are synthetic and stored in the browser. The demo does not run Flask/MySQL, create real rentals, process payments or model fleet availability. Customer vehicle references are descriptive records rather than enforced reservations. Multi-user concurrency and production access controls are outside this educational prototype.
technical: One frontend uses a Flask REST adapter or a browser-storage adapter. Existing /cars and /customer routes and integer Price fields are preserved; Price is presented as a whole-euro example daily rate. The MySQL adapter uses bounded pooled connections, parameterized queries, rollback and cleanup. Writes reject duplicate references/pairs and cross-origin requests. Tests cover both adapters, reset, failures and mobile layout.
run: Install requirements.txt, set DEMO_MODE=1 and run python CarServer.py. Open http://127.0.0.1:5000. See the README for MySQL configuration and opt-in disposable integration tests.

title: Breast cancer classification
alt: Measured classifier comparison with training-fold variability and explicit false-negative counts
desc: Compare three classifiers, inspect their mistakes and understand the limits of a single public dataset.
built: Refined the original educational investigation into an auditable comparison, with saved predictions, confusion matrices and a reproducible evaluation trail.
why: A useful model starts with understanding the data and evaluating it carefully. This investigation shows the steps between a dataset and an interpretable comparison.
how: Inspect the 569 source observations and retain all 30 numeric features, excluding identifiers and labels.
Use a deterministic stratified training/holdout split, with preprocessing fitted inside training-only cross-validation.
Compare errors on the same reused holdout, reconcile saved predictions with metrics and reproduce the figures.
demonstrates: Exploratory analysis, supervised learning, preprocessing, classifier comparison and critical interpretation of results.
caption: A reproducible three-model comparison using all 30 source features. Green bars show training-only cross-validation; brown points show the reused exploratory holdout.
result: All 30 features; 398 training examples; 171 examples in a repeatedly reused exploratory holdout. False negatives among 64 malignant-labelled holdout examples: Logistic regression 7, Decision tree 10, Random forest 6. Training-only five-fold cross-validation keeps preprocessing inside each fold. Saved predictions reconcile with the metrics and confusion matrices; repeated runs reproduce the same result files. No independent or clinical validation.
limits: This is educational analysis of a public teaching dataset, not a diagnostic system. The holdout has been reused across models and portfolio iterations, so it is exploratory rather than an untouched final test. No independent cohort, clinical validation, calibration study or causal interpretation is claimed. False negatives are shown explicitly.
technical: Seed 40; stratified 70/30 split; five stratified training-only CV folds; all 30 features. Logistic regression uses a StandardScaler pipeline; decision tree and random forest use fixed seeds. Saved prediction rows, labelled confusion counts, feature names, partition indices, dependency versions and dataset SHA-256 make the measured outputs auditable. Regression tests reconcile metrics and matrices and reproduce output files byte-for-byte.
run: Install requirements.txt, run python evaluate.py, python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v and python plot_portfolio.py. The original notebook remains available separately.

title: Hotel booking prototype
alt: Actual upgraded Express hotel homepage with date selection and illustrative licensed room photography
desc: A complete demonstration booking journey, from dates and room cards to guest details and confirmation.
built: Evolved my original Express/EJS hotel coursework into a polished application with a complete booking journey and a matching browser-based public demo.
why: A multi-step transaction should carry information reliably from one screen to the next. The project explores session state, validation and pricing across a booking journey.
how: Choose dates and a guest count, then compare three example room types.
Select room quantity and enter synthetic guest details; review the itemised total.
Confirm the demonstration and receive a clearly labelled demo reference. No real reservation or payment is made.
demonstrates: Server-rendered web development, session handling, input validation and turning a multi-step process into a working application.
caption: Actual local Express/EJS homepage. Room photography is licensed and illustrative; the fictional property, room catalog and prices are synthetic.
result: 15 automated hotel tests pass. Browser-tested the full Express journey and the matching static demo. Two €120 rooms over three nights total €720. The optional live MySQL test is skipped because no Docker/MySQL runtime is available.
limits: The public GitHub Pages demo runs in the browser, sharing the interface and rules with the server source. It does not run Express/MySQL. Neither mode creates real inventory, reservations, accounts or payments. The isolated MySQL setup is supplied but its live connection is not verified.
technical: A shared EJS shell, browser journey and pure booking-rules module power both modes. Express independently validates selections and guest details, recalculates prices from its catalog, protects session writes with CSRF tokens and handles duplicate confirmations. Optional MySQL uses a pooled synthetic catalog with safe errors. Original templates remain in views/legacy and Git history.
run: Run npm ci, npm test and npm start for Express at http://127.0.0.1:3000. No database is needed by default. npm run build:demo generates the public static version. An optional isolated MySQL Docker setup and opt-in integration test are documented separately.

title: Plant growth & statistics
alt: All thirty PlantGrowth observations shown by control and two treatment groups
desc: Explore thirty plant-growth observations, compare the groups and explain what the statistics can—and cannot—support.
built: Added a reproducible, visual PlantGrowth investigation alongside the original statistical coursework, preserving all raw observations and explaining uncertainty.
why: Differences in averages can be misleading without considering variability. This project shows how visual evidence and statistical testing support a careful comparison.
how: Inspect every observation under control and two treatment conditions, with ten examples per group.
Compare sample means and uncertainty; use Welch ANOVA as the primary omnibus comparison, with classic ANOVA shown as sensitivity analysis.
Examine three pairwise differences using Welch tests and a Bonferroni family adjustment, then interpret the small-sample limits.
demonstrates: Statistical reasoning, hypothesis testing, visual communication and explaining uncertainty around a decision.
caption: Ten source observations per group, with median/quartile boxes. Every point comes from the preserved PlantGrowth teaching dataset; visual jitter does not alter the measurements.
result: Thirty source observations, ten per group. Mean dried weights: control 5.032, treatment 1 4.661, treatment 2 5.526 (dataset units). Welch omnibus p=0.0174; classic equal-variance ANOVA p=0.0159 is shown as a sensitivity analysis. Pairwise comparisons use a three-comparison Bonferroni adjustment. Methods, assumptions and all observations are visible; this small teaching dataset does not establish general treatment effectiveness.
limits: Thirty observations in a teaching dataset do not establish universal treatment effectiveness. Independence and the original experimental design cannot be verified from the CSV alone. Mean intervals assume approximate normality; Welch inference is a small-sample approximation. A p-value is neither an effect size nor the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Methods were selected for this educational investigation, not preregistered confirmatory analysis.
technical: Source validation checks three groups of ten finite measurements. The reproducible script records dataset SHA-256 and dependency versions, computes Welch and classic one-way ANOVA, pointwise t intervals and three Bonferroni-adjusted Welch pair comparisons. Tests independently reconcile classic F with sums of squares, verify group summaries/multiplicity and reproduce numeric outputs byte-for-byte. Original notebook exercises remain intact.
run: Install requirements.txt, run python analyze_plants.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Results, raw source CSV and the original project.ipynb are available in the repository.

title: Sorting algorithms, measured
alt: Measured runtimes and observed interquartile ranges of five Python sorting implementations
desc: Measure five sorting implementations, then step through the work behind three of them in a simple interactive explorer.
built: Preserved five original Python algorithms and their confirmed tests, added traceable raw benchmark measurements and built a small browser explorer that shows real algorithm operations.
why: Two methods can produce the same answer while taking very different amounts of work. Correctness and measurement help make that trade-off visible.
how: Check every measured output against a trusted sorted result and compare five implementations on identical seeded inputs.
Record raw timings, medians and IQR with implementation hashes and environment details; reuse verified observations when the code is unchanged.
Step through instrumented bubble, selection and rightmost-pivot quicksort ports on the same starting values.
demonstrates: Algorithmic thinking, regression testing, reproducible experimentation and interpreting performance evidence.
caption: Five identical seeded random samples per input size. Lines show median measured milliseconds; bands show observed IQR, not confidence intervals. The recorded environment and exact implementation hashes accompany the data.
result: Five Python implementations passed correctness checks on 125 measured sorts: five identical seeded random samples at each size from 50 to 1,000. Median and IQR are calculated from saved raw measurements. Measurements were recorded on Windows-11-10.0.26300-SP0 with Python 3.12.2; unchanged algorithm hashes reuse those observations. The browser explorer illustrates operations separately and its animation speed is not a performance measurement.
limits: Measurements cover random non-negative integer inputs from 50 to 1,000 in one recorded environment; they do not establish a universal ranking. IQR describes observed variation, not confidence. Rightmost-pivot recursive quicksort has adverse-input recursion limits. Radix supports non-negative integers and rejects booleans/fractions. The browser explorer ports only three approaches and limits inputs to 24 values; animation pace is unrelated to Python runtime.
technical: Seven Python test methods preserve original correctness checks and validate raw timing aggregation, cache provenance and radix input domains. Three Node tests compare final traces with actual Python outputs, check permutation preservation at every step and reconcile known operation counts. The browser workflow exercises completion, controls, reset and mobile layout before publishing screenshots. Selection self placements are shown but do not count as index-changing swaps. Benchmark copies and correctness checks are excluded from measured timing.
run: Install requirements.txt; run python benchmark_portfolio.py, python plot_portfolio.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Use --refresh to request new measurements. For browser verification, build Python fixtures and docs, npm ci, npm run test:trace and npm run test:browser.

title: Iris dataset exploration
alt: Observed petal and sepal relationships for fifty flowers from each of three Iris species
desc: Explore three Iris species through authentic measurements, clear distributions and reproducible descriptive analysis.
built: Preserved the original Iris coursework and added a portable, tested visual investigation of all 150 supplied observations.
why: Before choosing a model, it helps to see how measurements vary and which features reveal useful structure. Clear exploratory analysis makes a dataset easier to understand.
how: Compare petal and sepal relationships using the observed species labels.
Inspect all four feature distributions, with every measurement visible and units in centimetres.
Compare species mean profiles and observed spread, then inspect the saved summaries and dataset provenance.
demonstrates: Data preparation, exploratory analysis, reproducible notebooks and selecting visuals that explain a pattern.
caption: All 150 supplied observations, fifty per species. The petal cluster for Setosa is distinct in this sample; the other species overlap. These colours represent observed labels, not predictions.
result: 150 supplied observations, 50 per species. Mean petal lengths: Setosa 1.462 cm, Versicolor 4.260 cm, Virginica 5.552 cm. Setosa forms a distinct petal cluster in these observations; Versicolor and Virginica overlap. All four measurements and all species labels are observed data, not model predictions. Repeated measurement rows are retained; this descriptive teaching sample does not establish general classification performance.
limits: This is descriptive exploration of a small, familiar teaching dataset. Separation in these observations is not independent validation of a classifier or evidence of general performance. Pooled correlations mix species and do not establish causation. Identical measurement rows are retained because equality alone does not prove duplicate sampling. The supplied CSV is preserved; historical Iris variants differ in two documented observations.
technical: A portable script validates the four positive finite measurement columns and three groups of fifty, records the input SHA-256 and software versions, and exports twelve feature/species summaries plus pooled correlations. Three tests reconcile summaries with independent raw-row calculations, validate provenance/counts and reproduce all numeric outputs. Standard-deviation bars describe observed variation, not uncertainty of the mean. Original analysis.py and Project.ipynb remain intact.
run: Install requirements.txt, run python explore_iris.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Inspect results/species-summary.csv, results/analysis.json and the preserved original notebook.
